title: Contains Duplicate
description: Brute force to optimized: pairwise comparison versus a hash set versus sorting for constant extra space.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Guest List for Repeats
blocks.text: Like scanning a sign in sheet at an event to see whether any name was written down twice. The moment a name that has already been seen shows up again, the answer is immediately yes.

blocks.caption: A repeated value anywhere in the array makes the answer true

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["The value 1 appears at index 0 and again at index 3","a duplicate exists"],["Answer","true"]]}
{"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Every value from 1 to 4 appears exactly once","no duplicate exists"],["Answer","false"]]}

blocks.text: With only a single element, there is nothing for it to repeat with, so the answer is always false.
This problem is worth comparing directly against Two Sum, to see exactly how much simpler "have I seen this before" becomes once there is no complement to compute.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is the same "have I seen this before" family already used for Two Sum, except here the question is even simpler, has this exact value appeared before, with no complement to compute at all.

Observation 2: Since only membership matters here, not a stored index or position, a hash set is the right structure, simpler than Two Sum's hash map, which needed to remember where each value was seen.

Observation 3: Testing nums equal to [1, 2, 3, 1] confirms it, the value 1 is recognized as a duplicate the instant it is seen a second time, with no need to compare it against every other individual element.

Observation 4: If memory is constrained but the array is allowed to be reordered, there is a second valid trade off entirely, sorting first brings every duplicate pair physically next to each other, trading the hash set's extra memory for a slower but more memory-frugal approach.
Recognizing this as a simpler cousin of Two Sum, needing only a set instead of a map, is what makes the hash based solution immediate rather than something to re-derive.
Compare every pair of elements directly, and if any two match, a duplicate has been found.

items: For every index i from 0 to n minus 1, look at every index j after i.
If nums[i] equals nums[j], a duplicate exists, return true immediately.
If no pair ever matches, return false.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop starts at i plus 1, so every pair is compared exactly once, with no element ever compared against itself.
The function returns true the instant any match is found, avoiding unnecessary comparisons once a duplicate is already confirmed.
Only a direct equality check is performed per pair, with no supporting data structure, since the brute force intentionally trades memory for simplicity.

blocks.text: This checks every possible pair, so any duplicate that exists is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), for the nested comparison of every pair.
Space: O(1), no extra data structure is used.

Limitation: re-comparing already examined values against every later value wastes almost all of the work. Once a value has been seen, checking whether it shows up again should not require rescanning the rest of the array from scratch.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair works but is wasteful: a value gets compared against every later value individually, even though all that ever matters is whether it has shown up anywhere before.

What stays the same as Two Sum: the underlying idea, remember what has already been encountered and check a hash structure directly instead of scanning.

What is simpler here than Two Sum: only membership needs to be tracked, has this value been seen, not a stored index or a computed complement, so a hash set is enough, a hash map is not needed.

Can a hash set answer "has this been seen" in constant time: yes, a single lookup replaces comparing against every later element individually.

The core idea: walk the array once, checking each value against a hash set before adding it, returning true the moment a value is already present.

Keep a set of every value seen so far while walking through the array once. For each new value, check whether it is already in the set. If it is, a duplicate has been found. Otherwise add it to the set and continue. Constant time average set lookups and insertions turn the pairwise comparison into a single linear pass.
Walk through the array once, checking each value against a hash set before adding it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Value","Already in set","Action"],"rows":[["1","no","add 1 to the set"],["2","no","add 2 to the set"],["3","no","add 3 to the set"],["1","yes","return true"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: one pass, checking a hash set before inserting each value

blocks.text: This works because checking the set happens before the current value is inserted, so a value is only ever reported as a duplicate once it has genuinely already appeared earlier in the array; since the set membership check and insertion both run in constant time on average, one full pass is sufficient to detect any duplicate that exists anywhere in the array.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current value is not yet in the set","It is inserted so future occurrences of it can be recognized","The scan continues, no duplicate found yet"],["The current value is already in the set","The function returns true immediately","No further elements need to be examined once a genuine duplicate is confirmed"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant time average set operations.
Space: O(n), for the set, which in the worst case (no duplicates at all) stores every element.
10. Further Optimization: Sorting to Trade Time for Space

The hash set uses O(n) extra memory. If memory is constrained but the array is allowed to be rearranged, sorting the array first brings every duplicate pair next to each other, so a single pass comparing each element to its neighbor is enough, using only O(1) extra space beyond the sort itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Array state","Result"],"rows":[["Sort the array","[1, 1, 2, 4]","duplicates are now adjacent"],["Compare index 0 and 1","1 equals 1","duplicate found, return true"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: sort first, then only neighboring elements need to be compared

items: Sorting the array first guarantees that if any two equal values exist anywhere in the array, they end up directly adjacent to each other.

A single forward pass comparing each element only to the one immediately before it is then enough to catch any duplicate, since no duplicate pair could ever be separated by a different value after sorting.
This trades the hash set's O(n) memory for the sort's O(1) extra space, at the cost of both a slower O(n log n) running time and permanently losing the array's original order.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra space beyond the sort itself (or whatever the sorting algorithm implementation requires), a real improvement over the O(n) hash set when the array may be reordered.

blocks.text: This problem is a clean example of the hash set membership pattern, and its further round shows the classic time versus space trade off between hashing and sorting.

items: Sorting the array when the original order actually needs to be preserved for a later step, without realizing the trade off being made.
Using a data structure that also stores counts when only membership (has this value been seen before) is actually needed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single element or an empty array","Both trivially have no duplicate."],["An array where every value is identical","Should return true the moment the second element is checked."]]}

blocks.text: Offer both the hash set and the sorting approach, and explain when each is preferable: hashing when the original order matters, sorting when memory is tight and reordering is acceptable.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid comparing every pair", think: a hash set answers membership in constant time, no complement or position needed.
If the interviewer says "what if memory is limited", think: sort first, then only adjacent elements ever need to be compared.
If the interviewer says "does the original order matter", think: hashing preserves it, sorting destroys it, ask which the situation actually requires.

Any problem offering a hashing versus sorting trade off, where hashing favors speed and preserving order, and sorting favors memory when reordering is acceptable.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: hash set membership checking, the simplest possible form of "have I seen this before", plus a classic time-versus-space trade off against sorting.

Core Idea: check each value against a hash set before inserting it, so any repeat is detected in a single linear pass; if memory is limited and reordering is acceptable, sorting first brings duplicates adjacent so a single neighbor-comparison pass suffices instead.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the hash set version, O(n log n) for the sorting version.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the hash set, O(1) extra for the sorting version.
Most Important Observation: membership alone calls for a set, not a map, a simpler tool than the one Two Sum needed.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force; offering both the hashing and sorting trade offs, and explaining when each applies, is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: hash set for membership when order matters, sort and compare neighbors when memory is tight.
